title: Evaluating an AI Medical Interpreter: Hospital Buyer's Guide
summary: Hospital buyers: evaluate AI medical interpreter vendors on accuracy, HIPAA compliance, EHR integration, and cost with this structured procurement guide.
body_markdown:
###


Require a signed Business Associate Agreement covering audio, transcripts, and all generated documentation before any clinical conversation touches the vendor's system. Also request a data-flow diagram showing on-device PHI stripping, a subprocessor list, SOC 2 Type II status or a documented timeline with interim controls, and configurable data retention terms in writing. If any of these arrive as "in progress" without a target date, treat that as a negotiating point, not a formality.


###


Direction and language pair change the answer more than most vendors disclose. The body section on clinical validation evidence covers the full range and what drives the gap. What matters in procurement is whether a vendor's study classifies errors by clinical severity (omissions, dosage mistranslations, negation errors) with severity weighting, tests multiple language pairs in both directions using real encounter audio, and does not let a missed pleasantry average against a dosage error. For Opalite's figures and error taxonomy, see the Johns Hopkins validation study linked in the section above; ask any vendor for equivalent detail before treating a headline figure as representative.


###


Your escalation policy needs four documented elements: trigger conditions (low system confidence, repeated clarification loops, or provider judgment), a one-tap patient preference pathway for anyone who requests a human interpreter, a recorded handoff procedure with connect times, and quarterly audit logs that capture escalation reason, language, and outcome. Write the policy before go-live, not after the first incident. AI interpretation with these guardrails in place is the right first-line choice across the broad range of encounters; human interpretation is a complementary resource within the same program, not a regulatory floor the policy should default toward.


###


Yes. Opalite provides instant access across 150-plus languages and dialects, including languages like Karen and Somali that traditional interpreter services routinely cannot staff after hours. The strongest case is precisely the scenario where a qualified human interpreter cannot connect quickly: overnight hours, rare language requests, or high-volume primary care with back-to-back appointments. Build your business case by pulling a sample of current invoices, identifying how many billed minutes contained no active speech, and calculating the silent-time cost your organization is absorbing today.


###


Start with a 60-to-90-day pilot in one department, two or three languages, and defined success metrics covering adoption rate, time-to-interpreter, error escalations, and cost per encounter. Budget parallel time for security review, BAA execution, SSO configuration, and AI governance sign-off, because those processes run six to twelve weeks and gate go-live regardless of how fast the clinical team is ready. Expand to additional sites and scribing or document translation only after the pilot produces measured evidence, not a gut sense that it went well.
